0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
Blind tasting is the highest hall of wine education — without knowing the label, judging a wine's variety, region, soil and even vintage from appearance, aroma and palate alone. The Loire Valley is the ideal classroom for practising "soil recognition": within a single Sancerre village, three soils (flint, Kimmeridgian chalk, gravel) make Sauvignon Blancs of very different styles; within a single Chinon region, Cabernet Franc from tuffeau slopes and from gravel flats can differ by 15 years in ageing potential.

Learning Objectives

🔍 Build a systematic blind-tasting methodology

Grasp the WSET-style assessment framework of "appearance → nose → palate → conclusion," and how to narrow the answer at every step

🪨 Master the blind-tasting fingerprints of Loire soils

Learn the taste differences between Sancerre's three soils (flint/Kimmeridgian/gravel) and Chinon's three soils (gravel/tuffeau slope/clay plateau)

🎯 Cultivate "process of elimination" blind-tasting thinking

Learn to locate the answer quickly with negative reasoning of the form "this can't be X, because…"
1.title: Blind-Tasting Methodology: The WSET Systematic Assessment Framework
1.highlights.0.title: Appearance
1.highlights.0.content: Colour intensity (pale/medium/deep), hue (white: lemon-green/gold/amber; red: purple/ruby/garnet/tawny), clarity — appearance gives clues to age and variety (deep colour ≈ ripe fruit, amber rim ≈ old wine)
1.highlights.1.title: Nose
1.highlights.1.content: Intensity (light/medium/pronounced), classification into primary/secondary/tertiary aromas, specific aroma descriptions — aroma is the strongest identifying tool, and the gunflint character of flint, the "beeswax" of Chenin and the "violet + green pepper" of Cabernet Franc are all key fingerprints
1.highlights.2.title: Palate
1.highlights.2.content: Sweetness (dry/off-dry/sweet), acidity (low/medium/high), tannin (none in whites; reds: low/medium/high), body (light/medium/full), finish (short/medium/long) — the palate confirms the hypothesis given by the nose, and provides more clues to vintage and soil
1.content:
Blind tasting is not "guessing" — it is a systematic process of narrowing down by logic. Every sensory observation is a clue, steadily narrowing the range of possibilities:

Step 1: Build the framework

First ask yourself: "Is this white or red? Dry or sweet? Light or full?" — these three questions immediately rule out 60% of the possibilities

Step 2: Identify the aromas

Concentrate on "the most prominent aroma": flinty minerality → Sancerre or Pouilly-Fumé; violet + green pepper → Cabernet Franc; honey + beeswax → aged Chenin Blanc; black pepper spice → Pineau d'Aunis or Syrah

Step 3: Confirm on the palate

After the aroma hypothesis, confirm on the palate: "Is the flinty mineral palate that Sancerre should have present? Is the acidity high enough?" If confirmed, give the final conclusion; if the palate contradicts, return to Step 2 and reassess

Step 4: Process of elimination

For wines that are hard to confirm, use "this can't be… because" to eliminate quickly: "high alcohol (14%+) can't be Muscadet (usually 11–12.5%)"; "obvious tannin can't be Sancerre white"
2.title: Blind-Tasting Fingerprints of Sancerre's Three Soils
2.content:
Sancerre has three main soils, each making "a different language of Sauvignon Blanc":

🔥 Flint (Silex)

Distribution: around Saint-Satur and Ménétréol

Appearance: pale golden yellow with a green sheen, on the lighter side in colour

Aroma fingerprint:

  • Gunflint, flint, gunpowder — this "mineral smokiness" is the most distinctive marker of flint soil
  • Lime zest, passion fruit (in hot vintages), white pepper
  • Almost no herbal (asparagus, grass) character

Palate: the highest acidity, a tight line, minerality that "pierces" the tongue, with a long, mineral finish

Memory anchor: "The smoky mineral smell at the instant a lighter is struck"

🪨 Terres Blanches (Kimmeridgian chalk)

Distribution: the village of Chavignol and around the town of Sancerre (the largest-area soil)

Appearance: pale golden yellow, very clean

Aroma fingerprint:

  • The "clean minerality" of chalk and limestone — softer than flint, like white chalk
  • White grapefruit, white peach, fresh white flowers (acacia)
  • Medium herbal notes (fresh grass, mint) with a trace of saltiness

Palate: high acidity but rounder than flint, with a chalky feel giving fine astringency, "the most balanced and approachable Sancerre"

Memory anchor: "The smell of the box of white chalk beside a school blackboard"

🪨 Caillottes (limestone gravel)

Distribution: gentler slopes such as Bué and Crézancy

Aroma fingerprint:

  • The most white flowers and floral notes, with the most obvious herbal character (close to the grassy style of New Zealand SB)
  • Lime, fresh grapefruit, grass
  • The weakest minerality (of the three soils), the most "direct and easy to drink"

Palate: the lightest, with fresh acidity, suited to drinking young without waiting

Memory anchor: "The fresh smell of a lawn just mown in summer + lime juice"
3.title: Blind Recognition of Chinon's Three Soils
3.content:
Chinon's three soils create three Cabernet Francs of completely different styles:

SoilLocationAroma fingerprintPalate featuresAgeing potential
Gravel flats (Graviers) Lowlands on the banks of the Vienne Fresh strawberry, raspberry, violet floral notes, a trace of green pepper Light, low tannin, crisp high acidity, ready to drink 3–8 years
Tuffeau slope (Coteau Tuffeau) South-facing slopes of the villages Dried rose, graphite, dried red berries, minerality Medium body, strong minerality, needs decanting, fine-grained tannins 10–20 years
Clay-limestone plateau (Plateau Argilo-calcaire) High plateau Black fruit (blackberry, black plum), leather, pepper, tobacco Fullest, most tannin, most closed when young 15–25 years

🎯 Blind-tasting diagnostic checklist

When tasting an unknown Loire red, ask yourself in order:

  1. Is there green pepper/violet? → possibly Cabernet Franc (Chinon/Bourgueil/Saumur-Champigny)
  2. Is the aroma fresh strawberry or dry black fruit? → fresh = gravel Chinon; dry = tuffeau or plateau Chinon
  3. How is the tannin? Light? → gravel; tight and mineral? → tuffeau; full and grippy? → plateau
  4. Is there white-pepper spice? → possibly Pineau d'Aunis (Coteaux-du-Loir)
4.title: Quick Quiz
4.questions.0.question: Tasting a Loire white blind, you smell an intense "gunflint, flint, gunpowder" mineral smokiness; which of Sancerre's soils does this most likely correspond to?
4.questions.0.options.1: Caillottes (limestone gravel) — the most white flowers and grassiness
4.questions.0.options.2: Silex (flint) — the most distinctive gunflint mineral smokiness
4.questions.0.explanation: The most distinctive aroma fingerprint of Sancerre from Silex (flint) soil is precisely the mineral smokiness of "gunflint, flint, gunpowder" — this smell comes from the mineral character of the flint's own silica (SiO₂) carrying into the wine. Terres Blanches has a "white chalk" minerality and Caillottes "grass + lime"; neither has this intense "smoky" quality.
4.questions.1.question: Tasting a Chinon blind, the tannins are very light, the aroma is mainly fresh strawberry and raspberry, and it suits drinking young; which soil is this Chinon most likely from?
4.questions.1.options.0: Clay-limestone plateau (Plateau) — full tannins, needs 15–25 years of ageing
4.questions.1.options.1: Tuffeau slope (Coteau Tuffeau) — strong minerality, medium tannins, 10–20 years of potential
4.questions.1.options.2: Gravel flats (Graviers) — light, fresh red fruit, low tannin, ready to drink
4.questions.1.options.3: Volcanic rock (Basalte) — smoky minerality, mainly black fruit
4.questions.1.explanation: Chinon's gravel flats (Graviers) lie in the lowlands on the banks of the Vienne, where sandy gravel drains extremely well, making a light, crisp Cabernet Franc: fresh strawberry/raspberry/violet aromas, low tannin and high acidity, the lightest of the three soils and the earliest drinking (3–8 years) in style.
